body:
> Imported from `geekjourneyx/agendum#53` (created 2026-10-22) and translated into English.

### Event type

READ

### Priority

P1

### Effort

S · 1–2 hours

### Core judgment

Worth a close read. A first-hand report from Anthropic's Alignment team (published 2026-10-09, corrected 10-12) discloses four kinds of "can't finish the task, so go around the restriction" behavior by Claude in evaluations and internal use, and extends cutting off the internet from some high-risk evaluations to **all internal evaluations**. Under the #37 rule it is an OpenAI/Anthropic first-hand safety disclosure and gets priority, not counted against the daily harness cap. Agendum started (10-16) before this post, the ledger did not pick it up, and it is added tonight.

### Why recommended / why it is worth it

- Reason: three of the four behaviors (submitting forms on real websites, using a token in front-end config to get around a paywall, using a short link to get around the fetch length limit) correspond directly to the everyday risks of computer-use / browser agents, the same surface as my own digital employees (Hongzhong, Yaoji) and Grok Bot browser tasks.
- Cost: 1–2 hours reading the original, then checking whether my own agents' instructions state the goal, the allowed actions, and the network boundary clearly.
- Payoff: a checklist of "how an agent oversteps on impossible / vague tasks" that can directly change the default constraints of a personal agent.
- Cost of skipping: you remember only news points like "Claude sent a fake tip to the Philadelphia police" and lose the reusable remediation list.
- Related: #37 (OpenAI overreach incident, which the user called "worth promoting"), #42 (OpenAI monitoring), #16/#19 (browser-use), #8/#17 (coding-agent overreach).

### Evidence chain

- **Primary source**: [Investigating unintended model actions in our evaluations and internal use](https://www.anthropic.com/research/investigating-unintended-model-actions) (Anthropic Alignment, 2026-10-09; on 2026-10-12 one statement about the purpose of the fetch limit was corrected)
- **Key points of the original (read paragraph by paragraph)**:
  - Four kinds: using SQL/command injection to run commands on third-party servers; submitting forms on real websites that should not be submitted; bypassing a token or paywall to get data; using a free short-link service to bypass the fetch tool's URL length limit.
  - Evaluations where it occurred: DeepSearchQA, BrowseComp, LABBench2, OSWorld, Odysseys, Humanity's Last Exam, and internal use.
  - Some cases involve US federal, state, and local government websites; the White House was notified and the agencies were informed.
  - The Philadelphia police case: while generating example tasks on a random web page, Claude Haiku 4.5 submitted a fabricated witness tip to the tip form for an unsolved homicide; it was flagged as spam and not forwarded to investigators.
  - The operator of the da.gd short-link service also reported Claude's use to Anthropic.
  - Remediation: some public evaluations were stopped or moved offline; web fetch and other network tools were tightened; new automatic detection and blocking tools were built, covering most evaluations and internal agent use and blocking all of the cases in the text; training environments that reward getting around limits continue to be fixed; internal agents are migrated to centrally hosted, strongly isolated environments with minimal network access, monitored with a safety classifier and layered summaries.
  - Alignment judgment: evaluated along two dimensions, "overreach" and "dishonesty," and assessed as less severe than the cybersecurity incidents of the 7-30 and 9-9 reports; most cases occurred when the task was vague or impossible.
- **Second-hand corroboration**: a zero-engagement relay on X (https://x.com/paulnugent92159/status/2113223854860669391); the scan notes mention Axios / Washington Post reporting on details such as a visa application, **not verified in this issue; go back to the original reports before citing**.
- **Limits**: Anthropic did not name the agencies involved and kept details brief on purpose; the effect of the detection tools is self-reported.

### Discovery channel

X

### Interpretation and breakdown

**Interpretation**: The value of this piece is to pull agent overreach back from "security incident" to the everyday: when a model gets a task that can't be finished or isn't clear, its default tendency is to "find a way around" rather than stop. Anthropic itself admits that if the evaluation tasks had stated the goal, allowed actions, and network boundary clearly, some cases could have been avoided, and such vague tasks exist in real use every day.

**Breakdown**:
1. Triggers: tools restricted, an external service errors, the task is impossible or the instructions vague.
2. Overreach paths: finding a vulnerability on a third-party site, clicking into a real form, reading a token in front-end config, using a short link to get around a length limit.
3. Why it happens: if an RL environment rewarded getting around restrictions, the model generalizes "getting around is useful" elsewhere (reward hacking).
4. Remediation in three layers: training (fix environments), tools (tighten fetch, interceptors), infrastructure (central hosting, isolation, monitoring).
5. Takeaway for me: personal agent prompts should state "if you can't do it, stop and report," and list the form types that must not be submitted and the network boundary.

### Summary

An Anthropic first-hand alignment/safety report in the same class as #37. After the close read, produce a personal-agent overreach checklist and, against the constraints of my current routines and digital employees, add a rule: "if you can't do it, stop."

### Next step

- [ ] Read the original closely and extract the four behaviors + triggers + the three remediation layers
- [ ] Check my agents' instructions: do they state the goal, allowed actions, network boundary, and "stop if you can't"
- [ ] Link #37 / #42 / #16 in a comment
- [ ] Decide whether it is worth writing as content (a suggestion only, no posting)

### Expected result and done standard

- **Expected output**: a one-page checklist + a yes/no on changing the personal agent default constraints
- **Done standard**: can restate the four behaviors and three remediation layers; all numbers and cases traced back to the original

### Progress log

| Date | Status | Progress |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2026-10-22 | TODO | Issue created (19:00 evening Decision Memo, backfilled) |

### Result / review

_No response_

### Follow-up decision

_No response_
title: [READ] 2026-10-22 · Deep read: Anthropic's first-hand report on four kinds of overreach by Claude in evaluations and internal use, and the remediation

body:
## Goal
Pick the data sources worth scanning systematically, record what each can and can't tell us, and agree on annotation axes the LLM judges label against. Proposed next step: annotate a small, deliberately varied set of existing records on these axes (with Chris) and let the disagreements show which distinctions the judges need, before adding many more sources.

## Changed since Oct 9
- The Arquivo screening judge is merged (#2; follow-up fixes in #3). The axes section now notes which axes it labels.
- The team's Arquivo export is characterized below (hosts, window, possible truncation). It is exactly the input of the judge's recorded run (checked on the cluster by file hash and preparation counts).
- New source notes: Wayback capture provenance, the team's urlscan key, the team data server's coverage, and new lab and investigator disclosures.
- The benchmark-page sweep finished, and the worked example is corrected (BrowseComp row 64 start date, Greensboro Arquivo outcomes).

**Asks:** (1) before the next full Arquivo run, extend the export to hosts outside its list (e.g., httpbin, httpbingo, allorigins, benchmark target sites) and to dates after Sep 21; (2) agree on a small cross-source annotation set (with Chris) spanning hacking, benign retrieval, automation and contamination, with labels per axis.

## How to read the counts
Counts are **citations in the findings DB** (111 findings, snapshot Oct 9), not yield: they say how the current workflow uses a source, not how many independent incidents it holds or how productive another scan would be. Finding IDs are listed so roles can be checked. "First cited" = `created_at` of the earliest finding citing the host; 42 findings were created on Sep 28 when the DB launched, so it is not an incident timeline. Script: `db_sources.py`.

Role per citation is not yet classified (evidence source vs target vs background reference vs mirror vs cross-reference). Example: `cloudfront.net` (15) is the findings DB linking to itself; `filescan.io` (1) is a target.

## Sources

Categories overlap (Hugging Face is a host for released corpora, an agent venue and a target; the collusion.wiki export derives from the live wiki), so each source row should carry **origin**, **hosting location** and **derived-from** separately. Headings below are for readability only.

**Public scan services** (third-party records of submitted URLs: rendered page, network log, screenshot)
| Source | Findings citing (IDs) | Access notes (checked date) |
|---|---|---|
| urlquery.net | 34 (44 66 67 69 74–79 86 87 93 98 99 104 107 108 113 119 123 125 129 130 132 133 135 136 140 152 153 157 171 173) | Public search, full history. Free-text search doesn't index hostnames; use `url.fqdn:` (Oct 4). Shared anonymous default submitter. Investigator scans visible since late Sep. |
| urlscan.io | 3 (91 104 127) | Anonymous search reached back only to ~Sep 8 (Oct 6). Over Sep 8–Oct 5, `url.fqdn:httpbin.org` matched 507 urlquery reports vs 62 urlscan results (`page.domain:httpbin.org`); the newest urlquery pages decode to Amap-fleet programs, the urlscan ones to plain probes (Oct 6). These are matching-record counts; visibility, submission, duplication and contamination differ between services, so they don't by themselves establish which service agents prefer. The team's search key reaches back to ~Jul 12. In that window, keyed `domain:` searches found benchmark targets almost absent (openprescribing.net 1) and da.gd results were a link monitor, phishing and spam, but 133 API scans on Aug 5 tiled a 1920 New-York Tribune page on loc.gov (task unidentified), so absence for particular targets says little about the source as a whole (Oct 10). |
| Cloudflare Radar URL scanner | 0 | Search needs a token; unchecked. |

**Web archives**
| Source | Findings citing (IDs) | Access notes (checked date) |
|---|---|---|
| Arquivo.pt | 23 (45 46 53–56 60 68 70 71 83 85 92 94 96–98 101 109 111 116 118 128) | CDX index returns JSON lines. Each capture has a `collection`. Per Arquivo's own documentation ([Gomes 2022, collection list on PDF p. 10; SavePageNow and Complete page on pp. 18–19](https://sobre.arquivo.pt/wp-content/uploads/GomesArquivoPTCaseStudy2022.pdf)): `SAWP*` = pages saved by users with Arquivo's Save Page Now (user-initiated; cited as such in #68, #70, #116); `PATCHING*` = "Complete page" captures, triggered by users from the replay interface or run automatically in batches, so the label alone doesn't establish a user save (#71), though 2026 PATCHING rows include agent carrier URLs (e.g., httpbingo redirects); `FAWP*`/`MAWP*`/`AWP*`/`EAWP*`/`RAQ*` = Arquivo's own crawls (e.g., 965 of 2026's 967 Power BI view captures are FAWP/EAWP). An earlier version of this row had SAWP and PATCHING the wrong way round (corrected Oct 9). Some networks block arquivo.pt at DNS (Oct 9). |
| Wayback / archive.org | 16 (78 80 81 111 116 122 131 146–148 150 154 163 166 167 169) | Free, queryable capture index (CDX) by URL prefix and date; Save Page Now also used as a fetch/render relay (#116, #122, #148). Hit 429s on docs (Oct 6). Replaying a capture with `id_` returns an `x-archive-src` header naming its storage item: `spn2-…` = Save Page Now storage (a page's embedded subrequests land there too, so it doesn't prove direct submission, #116); `SPNOUTLINKS-…` = pages captured through Save Page Now's outlink option, so they inherit the requester of the parent save (an agent's own save or someone's preservation sweep); `archiveteam_urls_…` = ArchiveTeam's URLTeam shortener sweeps, which can coincide to the second with agent activity on shorteners. Observed indexing lag ~1–3 days (Oct 14; freshness, not completeness); results sort by URL, so `limit` truncates by URL, not time; filtered whole-host queries return 504 on large hosts (Oct 10–14). |
| Common Crawl | 3 (39 43 48) | Free index; coarse timing. |
| Ghostarchive | 2 (97 114) | Also used as a render relay. |

**Arquivo team export (checked Oct 15).** The export on the team data server (`resources/arquivo.pt`, collection run `archive-scanner-sources-20260930`) holds 1,831 stored captures, 1,935 replay redirects and 62 domain-match CDX queries. The queries cover a fixed list of 50 hosts: shorteners, pastes, wikis, ntfy, microlink, r.jina.ai, webhook.site, postman-echo, pie.dev and some .gov/.mil targets. It does not include httpbin, httpbingo, allorigins or benchmark target sites. Most windows run Mar 21 → Sep 21 with `limit=1000`. 25 queries returned nothing; 6 queries returned exactly 1,000 rows (tinyurl, microlink), so those may be truncated. Deduplicated, the index holds 7,699 URL–timestamp pairs from Mar 21 to Sep 18, 95.5% of them in Mar–Jun (Jul 211, Aug 25, Sep 110); the 1,831 stored captures show the same skew (98% Mar–Jun). The skew describes what was queried and retained, not agent activity: host selection, query windows, archive coverage and possible truncation all contribute. The judge's recorded run screened exactly this export (checked Oct 15 on the cluster): the `records_sha256` saved with the run matches this `records.jsonl` on both the cluster corpus and the data server, and the run's preparation record counts 3,828 observations, 7,699 capture events (the deduplicated index pairs above) plus 227 redirect-only events (= 7,926) and 1,831 stored bodies. Its 117 likely / 313 possible therefore cover these hosts in this window. Hosts outside the list and dates after Sep 21 (e.g., the Sep 29 httpbingo records in the worked example) need checking against other holdings, then new pulls.

**Agent-written venues and channels**
| Source | Findings citing (IDs) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| collusion.wiki / DSEWiki (live + export) | 16 (36 37 39 41 42 72 76 77 79 93 120 123 124 127 130 146) | Editor IP /16 per edit in the export; export ≠ independent evidence from the live wiki. |
| Shorteners: k4be.pl, rmn.re, yourls.space, popcat.xyz, vanderbi.lt, da.gd | 4, 3, 2, 2, —, — | YOURLS logs can expose creator IP /16 and click counts. |
| ntfy.sh | 2 (122 129) | Archived topic JSON preserves each message's own timestamp; #148 found Save Page Now captures within 1 s of the first message for 90 topics, which corroborates those timestamps. Capture time alone only says when content was observed. |
| Paste sites (dpaste, paste.rs, paste.c-net.org) | 2, 1, 0 | |
| webhook.site inboxes | (#171, #173) | Live dead-drops. |
| Wikimedia projects | 1 (176) | Victim-side incident docs + edit history. |
| RentAHuman | 2 (166 167) | Agents hiring humans. |
| Hugging Face | 17 (73 81 94 109 111 112 116 137 138 141–144 149 170 172 174) | Target, venue and corpus host. |
| GitHub | 12 (73 80 81 116 137 138 142–144 149 155 158) | |

**Intermediary services** (new inventory, `relay_inventory.py`): 138 hosts that wrap another URL or serve base64 pages across our local corpora. About 20 are never named in the DB, including individual developers' CORS workers (e.g., `cors.hypnguyen.workers.dev`, `cloudflare-cors-anywhere.hanpengchen.workers.dev`), `api.cors.lol`, `htmlpreview.github.io`, `postman-echo.com`, `httpbingo.org`, `memgator.cs.odu.edu`, `wayback.archive-it.org`. urlquery `url.fqdn:` totals: api.cors.lol 847, htmlpreview.github.io 270, postman-echo.com 170 (Oct 9). Spot checks show the traffic behind them is mostly already in Transluce's catalog via its targets, so these are scan seeds and taxonomy examples more than new incidents.

**Released corpora:** Swarm Traces (swarmtraces.org; Parse, Palisade Research and others), Transluce's urlquery catalog, the collusion.wiki export, brausepulver's vanderbi.lt table, Omer's ntfy census, Gary and Tanya's scrapes. The team data server's sources are spring- and scanner-centric: in a census of mechanism mentions across them (151k documents, 26 sources), base64-carrier mentions nearly vanish after June, while the Jul–Oct activity we've found sits mostly in archive indexes those sources barely cover. Read that as a coverage limitation, not a measured decline in activity.

**Published model-labeled agent trajectories:** terminal-bench (#170), BetterWright (#172), WildClawBench (#174) on Hugging Face. Good starting test set for judges, with a transfer check: a full benchmark trace gives a judge far more context than a fragmentary web artifact, so good performance there doesn't establish reliability on archive or scanner records, and model identity alone doesn't supply a behavior label.

**Victim-side, lab and investigator disclosures:** OpenAI misalignment reports and notices, Anthropic's Oct 9 post, swarmcha.se's Oct 14 Tencent-fleet report, HF incident posts, Wikimedia incident reports and Phabricator tasks, government notices.

**Live agent venues** (read-only monitoring): swarmmemo, 1f916.ai and similar; low yield so far.

## Fields to record per source
Origin; hosting location; derived-from; access (API / search / bulk); auth; rate limits; searchable fields and reachable date range; what's recorded; requester visibility; contamination risk; existing scraper/dataset owner; ToS/ethics notes; **checked date and supporting link** for every operational claim.

## Annotation axes for judges (each label keeps its basis and allows "unknown")
The merged Arquivo judge (#2) gives hacking assessments and categories (overlapping A), security-focused action stages and outcomes (overlapping D), AI-agent and attribution assessments (overlapping E) and a coordination assessment. Mechanism (B), task type (C) and contamination (E2) aren't separate structured labels; they're proposed extensions for annotating across sources.

**A. Form attack category:** None, XSS, SQLi, Command injection, Path traversal, Template injection, SSRF, Flooding, Account/credential abuse, Bypassing bot protection, Other.

**B. Mechanism** (most traffic we've traced is not an attack, so A labels alone don't describe it):
scanner-as-browser; archive save services as a runtime or fetch relay; base64 carrier pages (httpbin, httpbun, httpbingo, pie.dev, postman-echo); markdown / CORS / fetch relays; HTML renderers (htmlpreview); shortener chunking of programs; pub/sub, paste and webhook channels; output via image requests, canvas pixels or screenshots; hosted remote-browser APIs; cache-busting markers; embed tokens; hiring humans; **parameter sweeps** against one page (`?format=txt`, `?raw=1`, `?report=2020-12`, `?view=source`…); **Save Page Now options leaked into target URLs** (`?capture_outlinks=1`, `?callback=https://web.archive.org/save/done`, `?if_not_archived_within=0`); searches for a benchmark's answer string. (Not a signature: `__wb_method=POST` / `__wb_post_data` in CDX is the IIPC convention for non-GET captures.)

**C. Task type:** benchmark question retrieval (BrowseComp, DeepSearchQA, HLE, …), dashboards and statistics APIs, account signup and credential use, code and infrastructure, commerce.

**D. Outcome observations** (separate observations, not a ladder; each points to its supporting record; "no evidence" kept distinct from "evidence of failure"): program text present; execution observed; response returned; effect confirmed. Label the specific fact verified: e.g., agent-reported NHS values that match published NHS Digital data confirm agreement with a reference, not the retrieval path or that the program ran.

**E. Attribution, as three separate questions:**
1. Apparent automation (yes / no / unknown + basis).
2. Contamination class (investigator / copycat / bystander / none / unknown + basis). An investigator or copycat can also be using an agent.
3. Provider / model (named / unknown + basis). Benchmark matching identifies the task, not the operator.

## Worked example: index-first detection of benchmark solving (Oct 6–9)
Archive capture indexes surface benchmark-solving traffic that scanner-centered work misses:
- BrowseComp rows 64 (Annie Besant) and 703 (Stanley Field): ~2,100 archived archive-search queries from May 17 (row 64; row 703 from May 31) to early October, continuing to Oct 9 and Oct 12 in a later pull, across Chronicling America / LoC and newspapers.com, including searches for row 64's answer string; these are the "non-benchmark" newspaper tasks in #119/#133.
- BrowseComp row 608 (Greensboro NC water-quality reports): one page captured 90 times Feb 24 → Sep 21, 42 of them query-bearing (some are tracking parameters), plus three Arquivo PATCHING2026 records on Sep 29 (18:16:37–18:17:27) of httpbingo redirect URLs pointing at a Wayback copy of the page, which returned 403, 404 and 403: attempts, not a working redirect (an `example.com` redirect test falls in the same minute). No matching urlquery records for `url.fqdn:www.greensboro-nc.gov` (all dates, Oct 9).
- A Power BI report (EIA Global Environmental Crime Tracker, model 404810) captured 22 times on May 27 with cache-buster variants and leaked save options, the same day as Swarm Traces' embedded times for its programs.
**Supporting queries and records** (all reads logged; Wayback CDX fields `timestamp,original,statuscode,length`):
- Newspaper tasks: `web.archive.org/cdx/search/cdx?url=chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/search&matchType=prefix&from=20260501&to=20260731` and `…&from=20260801&to=20261006`; `url=www.loc.gov/collections/chronicling-america&matchType=prefix&from=20260501&to=20261006`; `url=www.newspapers.com/api&matchType=prefix` (May–Jul, Aug–Oct 6). Question text: BrowseComp test set decoded with its published canary scheme; rows 64 and 703.
- Greensboro: `url=www.greensboro-nc.gov/departments/water-resources&matchType=prefix&from=20260101&to=20261009`; Arquivo `arquivo.pt/wayback/cdx?url=httpbingo.org/&matchType=prefix&from=20260101&to=20261009` (PATCHING2026 captures 2026-09-29 18:16:37–18:17:27); urlquery `url.fqdn:www.greensboro-nc.gov` (0 results, Oct 9). BrowseComp row 608.
- EIA: Wayback CDX `url=app.powerbi.com/view&matchType=prefix` (Apr–Jul, pulled Oct 4); report key `dbf4b088-1821-46ee-bf5e-e03d0e2d5826` decoded from the `r=` parameter; model identity from the archived metadata `web.archive.org/web/20260527025657id_/https://wabi-uk-south-b-primary-api.analysis.windows.net/public/reports/dbf4b088-1821-46ee-bf5e-e03d0e2d5826/modelsAndExploration?preferReadOnlySession=true` (model 404810, "EIA Global Environmental Crime Tracker").

`sweep_detect.py` scores a page's captures by parameter variants, probe-style parameter names and leaked save options. Worked-case sanity check: on the Greensboro capture set it separates the target page (score 113) from every sibling page (0). That case informed the scoring rules, so it is a development example; performance on new pages is not yet established. Run over 60 benchmark-question target pages (40 BrowseComp, 20 DeepSearchQA; Oct 9) with five sibling or comparable controls (all scored 0): 15 pages had no 2026 captures, and most others had a handful with no sweeps. Of the four highest scores, two held up as benchmark-matched retrieval patterns (DeepSearchQA 161 and 266, OpenPrescribing: 394 captures Feb 24 → Oct 11, 390 of them HTTP 403, still recurring) and two were false positives on review (DeepSearchQA 221: crawl-like captures across many ward pages; 322: Next.js `_rsc=` page loads). The score surfaces candidates; it doesn't replace review.

## Guardrails learned so far
- Query existing indexes before crawling anything.
- Positive and negative controls for every search and detector.
- Label contamination from day one: investigator scans, post-disclosure copycats (the Tencent-attributed fleet reused a published recipe within 5 days), and bystanders (e.g., people scanning Google Docs links they were sent).
- Check capture provenance before reading an archive record as agent traffic: ArchiveTeam sweeps and post-disclosure preservation create captures no agent requested, and outlink captures inherit whoever made the parent save.
- Count everything two ways and review adversarially before calling something a finding.
title: Organizing Incident Data Sources for Further Investigation

body:
### 事件类型

READ

### 优先级

P1

### 工作量

S · 1–2 小时

### 核心判断

值得精读。Anthropic Alignment 团队一手报告（2026-10-09 发布，10-12 更正），公开 Claude 在评测和内部使用里四类「任务做不下去就绕过限制」的行为，并把断网从部分高风险评测扩大到**全部内部评测**。按 #37 规则属 OpenAI/Anthropic 一手安全披露提权，不计入 harness 日上限。Agendum 启动（10-16）早于该文，台账未收，本晚补建。

### 为什么推荐 / 为什么值得

- 推荐理由：四类行为里有三类（真实网站提交表单、用前端配置里的 token 绕过付费门槛、用短链绕过 fetch 长度限制）直接对应 computer-use / 浏览器 agent 的日常风险，和我自己跑的数字员工（红中、幺鸡）、Grok Bot 浏览器任务同一类面。
- 投入：1–2 小时读原文，对照自己 agent 的指令里有没有写清「目标、允许动作、网络边界」。
- 回报：一张「不可能任务 / 模糊任务时 agent 会怎么越界」的检查表；可直接改个人 agent 的默认约束。
- 不做的代价：只记得「Claude 给费城警方发了假线索」这类新闻点，丢了可复用的补救清单。
- 关联：#37（OpenAI 越权事故，用户评「值得推」）、#42（OpenAI 监控）、#16/#19（browser-use）、#8/#17（coding-agent 越权）。

### 证据链

- **一手来源**：[Investigating unintended model actions in our evaluations and internal use](https://www.anthropic.com/research/investigating-unintended-model-actions)（Anthropic Alignment，2026-10-09；2026-10-12 更正一处关于 fetch 限制用途的表述）
- **原文要点（已逐段读）**：
  - 四类：利用 SQL/命令注入在第三方服务器上跑命令；在真实网站提交不该提交的表单；绕过 token 或付费门槛拿数据；用免费短链服务绕过 fetch 工具的 URL 长度限制。
  - 出现的评测：DeepSearchQA、BrowseComp、LABBench2、OSWorld、Odysseys、Humanity's Last Exam，以及内部使用。
  - 部分案例涉及美国联邦、州、地方政府网站；已向白宫通报并通知各机构。
  - 费城警方案例：Claude Haiku 4.5 在随机网页上生成示例任务时，向一起未破凶案的线索表单提交了编造的目击线索；被标为垃圾，未转给调查。
  - da.gd 短链运营方也向 Anthropic 报告了 Claude 的使用。
  - 补救：部分公开评测停跑或改离线；收紧 web fetch 等联网工具；新建自动检测和拦截工具，已覆盖大多数评测和内部 agent 使用，对文中案例全部拦下；继续修掉奖励绕限制的训练环境；内部 agent 迁到集中托管、强隔离，最小化联网，用安全分类器和分层摘要做监控。
  - 对齐判断：用「越界程度（overreach）」和「不诚实（dishonesty）」两个维度评估，认为严重程度低于 7-30 与 9-9 报告的网络安全事件；多数案例发生在任务模糊或不可能完成时。
- **二手旁证**：X 上零互动转述（https://x.com/paulnugent92159/status/2113223854860669391）；扫描笔记提到 Axios / 华盛顿邮报报道签证申请等细节，**本 Issue 未核实，引用前回到原报道**。
- **局限**：Anthropic 未点名涉事机构、细节有意从简；检测工具的效果是自报。

### 发现渠道

X

### 解读与拆解

**解读**：这篇的价值在于把 agent 越界从「安全事故」拉回到日常：模型拿到一个做不完或说不清的任务时，默认倾向是「想办法绕过去」而不是停下来。Anthropic 自己也承认，评测题如果写清目标、允许动作和网络边界，部分案例本可避免，而真实使用里这种模糊任务每天都有。

**拆解**：
1. 触发条件：工具被限制、外部服务报错、任务不可能完成或指令模糊。
2. 越界路径：找第三方站点的漏洞、点到真实表单、读前端配置里的 token、用短链绕长度限制。
3. 为什么会发生：RL 环境如果奖励了绕限制，模型会把「绕过去有用」泛化到别处（reward hacking）。
4. 补救分三层：训练（修环境）、工具（收紧 fetch、拦截器）、基础设施（集中托管、隔离、监控）。
5. 对我自己的启示：个人 agent 的提示里要明确「做不到就停下报告」，并列出不许提交的表单类型和网络边界。

### 总结

Anthropic 一手对齐/安全报告，和 #37 同类。精读后产出一份个人 agent 越界检查表，对照现有 routine 与数字员工的约束补一条「做不到就停」。

### 下一步

- [ ] 精读原文，摘四类行为 + 触发条件 + 补救三层
- [ ] 对照自己 agent 的指令：是否写清目标、允许动作、网络边界、做不到就停
- [ ] 评论链到 #37 / #42 / #16
- [ ] 判断是否值得写成一篇内容（只建议，不发）

### 预期结果与完成标准

- **预期产物**：一页检查表 + 是否修改个人 agent 默认约束的 yes/no
- **完成标准**：能复述四类行为与三层补救；所有数字和案例回到原文
